client: I've been really struggling ever since I got laid off from my tech job back in February. The financial pressure is just constant — I check my bank account and feel this wave of dread every single time. And honestly, I can't even bring myself to sit down and update my resume, which I know I need to do, but something just stops me every time I try.
therapist:
It makes complete sense that you're feeling this weight — losing your job is a genuinely difficult experience, and that dread when you check your account sounds exhausting to carry every day. I'm also noticing something really interesting: you *know* updating your resume would help, yet something pulls you away each time you try, which tells me there might be more going on beneath the surface than just procrastination. 

When you imagine yourself sitting down to work on that resume, what's the first thought or feeling that comes up for you?

client: Honestly, the first thing that comes up is this feeling of... like, what's even the point? I spent six years building up my career at that company and they just cut me loose in a ten-minute Zoom call, so part of me wonders if putting all that effort into a resume is just setting myself up to get hurt again. It's like my brain is trying to protect me from something, but it's also keeping me completely stuck.
therapist:
That insight you just shared is really profound — your brain *is* trying to protect you, and that makes complete sense after experiencing something that felt so dismissive of six years of your dedication and hard work. What you're describing sounds like a painful automatic thought: "If I try, I'll just get hurt again," which is your mind generalizing one very real wound into a prediction about the future. 

I'm curious — when you think about those six years of experience and what you actually built, what do *you* believe that says about your worth, separate from what that ten-minute Zoom call seemed to say?

client: I mean, rationally I know I did good work there — I led projects, I mentored junior developers, I actually built systems that are still running in their infrastructure right now. But when I try to hold onto that and feel good about it, there's this other voice that immediately jumps in and says "well, it clearly wasn't good enough, was it?" And that voice is honestly a lot louder than any logical argument I can make to myself.
therapist:
That critical inner voice can feel so overpowering, especially when you're already hurting — but I want to gently point something out: a company making a financial decision during layoffs isn't actually evidence that your work wasn't good enough, and the fact that your systems are *still running in their infrastructure* is a pretty powerful counter-argument sitting right there. What you're describing is a really common CBT pattern where our emotional mind shouts and our rational mind whispers, and the good news is that we can gradually work on turning up the volume on that quieter voice.

When that critical voice says "it clearly wasn't good enough," whose voice does it remind you of — is it new, or does it feel familiar from somewhere earlier in your life?

client: That's... actually a question I wasn't expecting, and it kind of stopped me for a second. I think it does sound familiar — my dad was never really satisfied with anything I did growing up, like I could get a B+ and he'd ask why it wasn't an A. But I'm not sure I totally buy the connection between that and what's happening now — I mean, isn't this just about the job situation, or are you saying my whole reaction is really about my dad?
therapist:
That's a really fair pushback, and I want to be clear — your pain about the job is absolutely real and valid completely on its own terms. What I'm gently suggesting isn't that this is "really about your dad" instead of the job, but that growing up with a voice that moved the goalposts no matter how hard you tried may have laid down a groove that makes *this* particular kind of rejection land even harder than it might otherwise.

It's like the layoff handed that old critical voice a megaphone. Does that distinction feel any different to you — that both things can be true at once?

client: Yeah, when you put it that way — the megaphone thing — that actually does land differently, and I kind of hate that it makes sense because it means this is more complicated than just finding a new job. Like, even if I land something tomorrow, that voice might still be there telling me it's only a matter of time before they figure out I'm not enough. I guess I just never really connected those two things before, and it's a little unsettling to sit with.
therapist:
It takes real courage to sit with something unsettling rather than push it away, and the fact that you're willing to do that right now says something important about you. You've just named something that many people spend years not seeing — that the job search isn't just a practical problem, but that there's also this deeper story running underneath about whether you're ever truly "enough," and awareness of that is genuinely the first step toward loosening its grip. 

The good news is that voice isn't a life sentence — but I'm curious, now that you can see it a little more clearly, what would it mean for you if you could start to separate *your* sense of your own worth from whether any particular employer, or your dad, ever fully recognized it?

client: Honestly, it sounds really freeing in theory, but I'm not sure I even know what that would feel like — like, my whole life I've kind of measured myself by external results, grades, performance reviews, whether my manager seemed happy with me. If I take all that away, I'm not sure what's left to tell me I'm doing okay. It's a little scary to think about building that from scratch, especially when I'm already feeling so destabilized by the whole job loss thing.
therapist:
What you're describing - that fear of an internal void if you remove all the external measuring sticks - is one of the most honest and human things a person can recognize about themselves, and it makes complete sense that it feels scary, especially when you're already on shaky ground. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: you're not actually starting from nothing, because that person who led projects, mentored others, and built systems that are still running — he was making judgments and choices and showing up every day, and *something* inside was guiding all of that, even if you've never been given credit for trusting it. 

What's one small moment, even recently, where you made a decision or acted in a way that felt right to you — not because someone approved of it, but just because it aligned with something you valued?

client: There was actually this moment a few weeks ago where a former colleague asked me to review his code for a side project he was working on, and I spent like two hours giving him really detailed feedback even though I had no obligation to and nobody was going to grade me on it. I did it because I genuinely wanted to help him and I knew I could. But even as I say that, my brain is already trying to minimize it — like, "that's not a big deal, that's just what decent people do," which I guess is kind of proving your point about that voice.
therapist:
You just caught that voice in real time, minimizing something meaningful before you could even fully feel it — and that self-awareness is actually remarkable. What you described *is* exactly what decent people do, but here's the thing: you chose to spend two hours helping someone using skills you'd built over years, with no external reward, purely from an internal sense of capability and care — and that *is* your own compass working, even when everything else felt destabilized.

I'd love for you to sit with that memory this week as a small piece of evidence against the "not enough" story — not to fix everything, but just to notice it's there. What do you think it would take for you to let that kind of moment count as real proof of your worth, even just a little?

client: I want to let it count, I really do, but I think the honest answer is that one moment feels too small to push back against years of that voice — like, my brain is already telling me I'll remember it for a day and then forget it when the next rejection email comes in from a job application. I guess I'm also a little skeptical of the "collect evidence" approach in general, because it feels like I'm just trying to logic my way out of something that doesn't really respond to logic. Is there something more... I don't know, substantial that actually shifts this over time?
therapist:
Your skepticism is actually really healthy and worth honoring — you're right that this voice wasn't built by logic, so it can't be fully dismantled by logic alone, and the "collect evidence" approach is just one small tool, not the whole answer. What tends to create more substantial shifts over time is a combination of things: building new *experiences* that contradict the old story (not just thoughts about them), and often doing deeper work on where that voice originally came from — which is exactly the kind of thing that can be hard to sustain alone and where working with a therapist consistently over time can make a real difference. 

I'm curious — have you ever had any space, whether therapy or otherwise, where you've been able to explore that older story about never being enough, or has this kind of conversation been pretty rare for you?

client: Honestly, this kind of conversation is pretty rare — I've never done therapy before, and most of the people in my life, my friends, my family, they're more the "just keep pushing, you'll land on your feet" type, so nobody really goes here. And I'll admit this conversation has been more useful than I expected it to be, but I also feel a little exposed right now, like we've pulled back a curtain on something I've been carrying for a long time without realizing it. I guess my hesitation is whether I can actually commit to this consistently when I'm already overwhelmed by the day-to-day financial stress — it feels like a lot to take on at once.
therapist:
That feeling of exposure makes complete sense — you've just seen something real about yourself that's been quietly running in the background for decades, and that's a lot to hold, especially when you're also worried about paying your bills. I want to acknowledge something though: you showed up to this conversation, you went deeper than you expected to, and you stayed honest even when it got uncomfortable — and that's not nothing, that's actually the same quality that made you spend two hours helping your colleague for no external reward.

The financial stress is real and won't wait, and the inner work is real and matters — and I don't think you have to choose between them or tackle everything at once. What would feel like a manageable first step that honors both — something small enough to not add to the overwhelm, but meaningful enough to feel like you're actually moving?

client: I've been sitting here thinking about that question and the honest answer is that maybe the most manageable thing would be to just open my resume file — not even edit it, just open it and look at it for five minutes without any pressure to make it perfect. But even as I say that, I'm aware that last time I tried something like that I ended up closing the laptop after thirty seconds because the anxiety just spiked immediately, so I'm not totally confident it'll go differently this time. I guess what I'm asking is — if that happens again, does that mean I'm failing at this, or is that just part of the process?
therapist:
Closing the laptop after thirty seconds would not mean you're failing — it would mean you're a person with a nervous system that learned to protect itself, and that protection is doing exactly what it was trained to do. The fact that you're already anticipating the anxiety spike and asking this question ahead of time actually tells me you're approaching this more thoughtfully than before, and even thirty seconds of having that file open would be thirty seconds more than last time.

What if we reframed the experiment slightly — instead of measuring success by how long you stay with it, you just notice what thought or feeling causes you to want to close it, and bring that back here? What do you think that anxiety is actually trying to protect you from in that moment?
